sections.h2: Pickens County housing at a glance
sections.html:
The northwest corner of South Carolina belongs to Pickens County. Its seat is the city of Pickens, its biggest community is Easley, and Clemson, Liberty, Central, Six Mile and Norris are the other municipalities. The 2020 census counted 131,404 residents.

Educational services, led by Clemson University, supply 21.4% of local jobs. The housing that results includes rentals around Clemson, inherited houses in Easley and Pickens, and mountain properties near the northern edge that are costly to keep up. Each carries a different tax question.

The county Treasurer takes current property tax from October 1 through March 16, though the penalty-free deadline is January 15. Vehicle tax can be paid any time of year. Escrow bills for mortgaged homes are mailed near October 1, and lenders usually pay before the end of December. For mailed checks, the postmark is the payment date.

OfficeAddress and phoneHours
Treasurer222 McDaniel Avenue, B-6, Pickens, SC 29671; (864) 898-58838:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday to Friday
Delinquent Tax222 McDaniel Avenue, B-15; (864) 898-5890Call to confirm

Look for the County Health Department off Highway 178 and you will find the right building. Bring the property address with you. Owners who live outside the county can phone for a figure and send payment by mail to the same address, which saves a trip when a closing date is close.

The Treasurer sits behind the County Health Department off Highway 178. At the counter you can use cash, a check or a money order. Mail goes to that same street address, and the office sends a receipt back.

Late charges under S.C. Code 12-45-180 are 3% after January 15, 7% more before February 2 and 5% more before March 17. Whatever is still open after the March 16 window passes to the Delinquent Tax Office, which collects under Chapter 51 of Title 12 and runs the county tax sale.

A payoff taken during these weeks includes penalties and costs, and it moves whenever a penalty date arrives, so get it early.

A year with a Notice of Valuation gives you 90 days from its mailing to object in writing. A year without one means filing before the first penalty date, which applies to this year's bill, while a later filing applies to next year's.

  1. Informal review: an appraiser examines each appeal filed on time.
  2. Notice of Decision: the result comes by mail from the Assessor.
  3. Board of Assessment Appeals: give the Assessor written notice inside 30 days of the decision date.
  4. Administrative Law Judge Division: the next appeal is due 30 days after the Board's written decision.

Faxed appeals are refused, and the Assessor is the only office that can accept one. Anyone acting for the owner needs a signed authorization or power of attorney. Late or misdirected filings risk dismissal. The Assessor's number is (864) 898-5872.

Recording a deed can start a fresh valuation, even for a gift. The Assessor's term is Assessable Transfer of Interest, and the new value is fair market value on December 31 of the transfer year. Countywide, the last reassessment took effect December 31, 2018, and appeared on 2019 notices. S.C. Code 12-43-217 calls for reappraisal each fifth year, with a Notice of Valuation whenever a value climbs by $1,000 or more. Phone the Assessor for the next cycle.

The December 31 owner is responsible for that year's tax, and the lien stays with the land. Settle the bill at closing so the buyer starts with a clean slate.

Primary homes occupied by their owners are assessed at 4%, and everything else at 6%. New owners apply to the Assessor once the deed records and they move in, ahead of the first penalty date.

A trust transfer calls for a new application, and the 4% rate is dropped unless the income beneficiary lives there as a primary residence and the trustee certifies it. Failing to report lost eligibility within six months can bring a penalty up to 100% of the tax paid, with interest.

Check your status before listing an estate or a rental. A change from 4% to 6% lifts the bill a buyer will see.

At closing, the state's deed fee applies: $1.85 for each $500 of value, of which $1.30 goes to the state and $0.55 to the county. A deed in lieu of foreclosure is exempt. See S.C. Code 12-24-10 and 12-24-40.

sections.h2: If taxes are owed and you want to sell
sections.html:
Inherited houses, tired rentals and mountain homes that are hard to maintain make up most Pickens County sales with a tax problem. Four offices matter:

  • Treasurer: (864) 898-5883, current bill.
  • Auditor: (864) 898-5895, personal property and homestead exemption.
  • Assessor: (864) 898-5872, rate and value.
  • Delinquent Tax: (864) 898-5890, anything past March 16.

Unpaid tax is paid out of the proceeds by the title company. Cash Home Buyers purchases houses as they stand, which spares an older or damaged house from repair work. Phone these offices, gather the numbers and weigh them against any offer.

sections.h2: What to ask each office before you list
sections.html:
Give the Treasurer your address and ask what is open and what a payoff would be on your target date. Ask the Assessor which rate the house carries and whether a transfer resets the value. Ask Delinquent Tax if any year has been sent over. Date every answer you write down.

Heirs have one more question to ask: is the 4% rate still attached? It may not survive a change of name, and that answer often explains why a buyer's tax estimate comes in above the old bill.

sections.h2: Timeline for a Pickens County sale
sections.html:
Work back from three dates: January 15, February 2 and March 17. Closing ahead of January 15 pays just the base bill, a closing in the next few weeks adds the first penalty, and every later date adds another. Once March 16 has gone by, the account sits with Delinquent Tax and that office supplies the payoff.

Request the payoff when the contract is signed instead of the day before closing. An outdated figure can hold up funding. Hand the title company both office numbers so it can verify directly.

Landlords around Clemson get squeezed from two sides: worn units that a mortgage lender may balk at, and a 6% rate that makes each January bill heavier. Selling for cash, with no repairs, answers both.

Owners thinking of renting the house out before selling should know that rental use pushes the rate toward 6%, and the buyer's lender will see that higher bill.

Houses passing through an estate or trust need extra care. The 4% rate can fall away at transfer, and a new application follows once the new owner lives there. The Assessor can describe the paperwork a trustee needs to certify that the income beneficiary lives in the home.

Since the year's tax follows the December 31 owner, the family should agree on who pays before the deed is recorded. A brief note to the title company on how the bill will be split avoids arguments at the table.

sections.h2: Quick directory for Pickens County sellers
sections.html:
Four counters cover almost every question. Start with the Treasurer for a current bill, then the Assessor if you think the rate or value is wrong. The Auditor deals with homestead exemption and personal property. Delinquent Tax takes over once an account is past the collection window.

The Treasurer and Delinquent Tax share the McDaniel Avenue address, with suites B-6 and B-15, so one visit can answer both a current-year question and a past-due one. Take notes on each conversation, and give your title company the written payoff once you have it.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to pay Pickens County property tax without a penalty?
faqs.a: January 15. The Treasurer accepts current-year payments from October 1 through March 16.

faqs.q: Where is the Pickens County Treasurer's office?
faqs.a: 222 McDaniel Avenue, B-6, Pickens, SC 29671, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays. Call (864) 898-5883.

faqs.q: How do I contest a Pickens County value?
faqs.a: Object in writing to the Assessor within 90 days of the Notice of Valuation. A decision can be taken to the Board of Assessment Appeals within 30 days, then to the Administrative Law Judge Division.

faqs.q: Does a sale reset the assessed value in Pickens County?
faqs.a: It can. A recorded deed may count as an Assessable Transfer of Interest, valued as of December 31 of the transfer year.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Pickens County home that has unpaid taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, because the title company pays the tax from your proceeds. Cash Home Buyers can buy the house as it is. For a payoff, call Delinquent Tax at (864) 898-5890.
